steps.title: Taking the request

steps.body: This diagram is CodeFlow's own pipeline, drawn by the renderer it describes. Follow the line down the middle - that is one request being turned into a map.
steps.detail: The gateway owns no analysis logic. It authenticates the request, then orchestrates four other FastAPI services and persists what comes back.

node.label: POST /analyse
node.oneLiner: A user asks CodeFlow to map a repository.

steps.title: CodeFlow, mapping itself

steps.body: The first real branch. One arm ends the story immediately; the other commits to four minutes of analysis. Notice the branch that stops, and the one that rejoins.

branches.label: cold
branches.note: Every stage below has to run.

steps.detail: Maps are keyed on (user_id, repo) and upserted, so re-running a repo replaces its map rather than accumulating rows.

node.label: Repo already mapped?
node.oneLiner: Neon is checked for a stored map before anything is re-analysed.

steps.title: Decision - is this repo already mapped?

steps.body: The gateway hands the repo to the profiler, tracer, layout and render agents, one HTTP hop each, and stitches their JSON back together.
steps.detail: Gateway to tracer and layout timeouts are 900s, because a cold trace of a large repo genuinely takes minutes.

node.label: Fan out to the agents
node.oneLiner: Profiler, tracer, layout and render - one HTTP hop each.

steps.title: Five services, one orchestrator

steps.body: One environment variable decides whether the same code talks to four processes on this laptop or to four containers on Railway. Both arms rejoin the main line.
steps.detail: `.env` is not hot-reloaded, so the gateway has to be restarted after changing it - a small thing that has cost real debugging time.

node.label: ENVIRONMENT = local?
node.oneLiner: The same code targets localhost or Railway.

steps.title: Decision - localhost or Railway?

steps.body: Static analysis builds a symbol table, resolves every call, and turns each branch point into a candidate decision.

node.label: Reading the code
node.oneLiner: Static analysis builds a symbol table, resolves every call, and turns each branch point into a candidate decision.

steps.title: Reading the code

steps.body: Every function in the repo becomes a symbol, and every import is resolved to a real file. This is the foundation the whole call graph stands on.

branches.label: code
branches.note: One file at a time: parse, then bucket classes and functions.

steps.detail: Source roots are derived from where imports actually bind, never from directory names. Assuming a folder was called 'agents' once resolved almost every internal call to 'ext:' and shredded the entire call graph.

node.label: 1 - Index the repo
node.oneLiner: Function-level symbol table for the whole repo.

steps.title: Stage 1 - index every symbol

steps.body: Ancestor prefixes are walked longest-first, so any directory layout works. Only the project arm rejoins the line; the other two genuinely stop here.
steps.detail: This exact function has been the site of two outages. Both were the same bug: hardcoding this repo's own folder names into the resolver.

node.label: Where does this import resolve?
node.oneLiner: Longest-prefix ancestor walk, stdlib short-circuited.

steps.title: Decision - project, stdlib, or third party?

steps.body: Each call site is bound to a target, carrying the control context it sits inside - which if, which except, which loop.

branches.label: code
branches.note: Control context - scope, local bindings, self types - travels with the call site.

steps.detail: The control context is what later lets a fork be described as a decision rather than just a branch instruction.

node.label: 2 - Resolve the call graph
node.oneLiner: Call graph with per-call-site control context.

steps.title: Stage 2 - resolve the call graph

steps.body: Confidence is recorded, never guessed away. An inferred edge is drawn faded on the final diagram rather than being quietly promoted to a fact.
steps.detail: Both arms rejoin the line - an uncertain edge is still an edge.

node.label: Can the target be resolved statically?
node.oneLiner: Confidence is carried through to the picture.

steps.title: Decision - resolved or inferred?

steps.body: The heart of it. Static analysis finds every branch point in the repo and sorts it into one of seven shapes. Watch all seven arms converge back into the main line.
steps.detail: Static analysis owns structure. The LLM that runs two stages later may judge these forks and label them, but it may never add, remove, merge or rewire a single one.

node.label: 3 - What kind of fork is this?
node.oneLiner: Seven kinds of branch point, no exceptions.

steps.title: Stage 3 - extract every fork

steps.body: Seven effect kinds hang off the line as annotations. These become the icons on the diagram, and they are what makes cross-service stitching possible later.
steps.detail: Effects are annotations, not control flow, so these branches stop rather than rejoining. A call made inside a third-party SDK produces no effect - a known and deliberate blind spot.

node.label: 4 - Detect side effects
node.oneLiner: http, db, llm, file, queue, email, response.

steps.title: Stage 4 - what touches the outside world?

steps.body: The only stage an LLM touches: it judges which forks a human would actually put on a mental model, and never rewires the graph.

node.label: Deciding what matters
node.oneLiner: The only stage an LLM touches: it judges which forks a human would actually put on a mental model, and never rewires the graph.

steps.title: Deciding what matters

steps.body: Structure is already fixed. The model's entire job is to decide which of those forks a human would actually reason about, and to write the question each asks.

branches.label: code
branches.note: Batches representatives, then fans the verdict back out to every duplicate fork sharing that fingerprint.

steps.detail: Three decisions in a row follow: which judge runs, whether the answer is already cached, and what the verdict is.

node.label: 5 - Judge significance
node.oneLiner: Which forks are decisions a human would care about?

steps.title: Stage 5 - the only place an LLM is allowed

steps.body: With no API key the system does not fail - it degrades to a deterministic reach heuristic. Both arms rejoin the line, so the pipeline always completes.

branches.label: key set
branches.note: Batches ~20 forks per call at temperature 0.

steps.detail: This is why the whole pipeline can be run and tested with --no-llm, and why a missing key is a downgrade rather than an outage.

node.label: Is an API key present?
node.oneLiner: No key means a deterministic offline judge.

steps.title: Decision - LLM or heuristic?

steps.body: Verdicts are content-addressed on the fork's source, its arm labels and its reach sizes. This one branch is the difference between four minutes and three seconds.
steps.detail: The fingerprint includes a PROMPT_VERSION. Change the prompt without bumping it and stale verdicts are silently served - so the cache is only safe because that version is part of the key.

node.label: Has this fork been judged before?
node.oneLiner: Content-addressed verdict cache.

steps.title: Decision - is the verdict already cached?

steps.body: The verdict that matters. A decision becomes a diamond with a human question on it. Noise takes the branch that stops - demoted to a deeper level, never deleted.

branches.label: decision
branches.note: A diamond, labelled with a question.

branches.label: guard
branches.note: Real, but not a choice - a validation gate.

branches.label: noise
branches.note: Demoted to a deeper level, never deleted.

steps.detail: Labels like 'User can access ticket?' come from this stage. Nothing is ever deleted to make the page fit; it is only ever pushed further down.

node.label: Decision, guard, or noise?
node.oneLiner: The verdict that decides what reaches the diagram.

steps.title: Making it fit

steps.body: Judged forks are projected onto the node kinds you have been looking at all along: entry, step, decision, parallel, effect and outcome.
steps.detail: This is where the diagram's vocabulary is fixed. Straight-line step chains are merged here so the picture is not padded with pass-through boxes.

node.label: 6 - Condense to a FlowGraph
node.oneLiner: Projection onto entry/step/decision/effect/outcome.

steps.title: Stage 6 - condense to a graph

steps.body: An arm that stops has to be given an honest ending rather than trailing off the page. Fittingly, one of these two branches stops and the other carries on.

branches.label: reaches code
branches.note: Points at the next real node.

branches.label: terminates
branches.note: An honest ending, not a loose edge.

steps.detail: OutcomeLabeler names the dead end Returns, Raises or Continues - or uses a label the judge supplied.

node.label: Does this arm reach further code?
node.oneLiner: Arms that terminate get a named outcome.

steps.title: Decision - does this arm go anywhere?

steps.body: An outbound HTTP call in one service and a route in another are the same edge. This is the stage that turns four separate graphs into one system.
steps.detail: Without this, a microservice repo renders as several disconnected islands.

node.label: 7 - Stitch the services together
node.oneLiner: Outbound calls matched to route entries.

steps.title: Stage 7 - join the services up

steps.body: Deterministic URL matching goes first. Only what is left over is put to the model, and those edges are drawn faded because they are inferred, not proven.

branches.label: unresolved
branches.note: Judged, and drawn as an inferred edge.

steps.detail: The same discipline as everywhere else: the cheap deterministic path runs first, and the LLM is the fallback rather than the default.

node.label: Does the URL match a known route?
node.oneLiner: URL matching first, the model only for leftovers.

steps.title: Decision - matched, or judged?

steps.body: The rule that shapes every CodeFlow diagram: the first view of a codebase is at most 15 nodes. Nothing is deleted to achieve that.
steps.detail: A node's hidden_children is exactly what its + reveals. A + that opens 50 nodes at once is treated as a bug, not as disclosure.

node.label: 8 - Budget the page
node.oneLiner: Nothing is deleted - detail is demoted.

steps.title: Stage 8 - fit the page without losing anything

steps.body: When the page is over budget the low-ranked nodes move behind a + on their parent. Both arms rejoin: whichever way it goes, the node still exists.

branches.label: over budget
branches.note: Moves behind a + on its parent.

steps.detail: This is the difference between a summary and a lie. Every node in the original graph is still reachable from the rendered page.

node.label: More than 15 nodes on top?
node.oneLiner: Over budget means demoted, not dropped.

steps.title: Decision - demote, or keep?

steps.body: A sequence chains; a decision's arms are mutually exclusive alternatives. This is derived from the body's actual shape - it is not asserted.
steps.detail: Asserting single-entry as an invariant crashed the pipeline on CodeFlow's own repo: a shared memoized node can legitimately be both a predecessor of a body member and a containment ancestor of it.

node.oneLiner: Derived from shape, never asserted.

node.label: Drawing it
node.oneLiner: The server owns geometry; the browser is a thin renderer with progressive disclosure.

steps.title: Drawing it

steps.body: Every x and y on this page was computed in Python and shipped as JSON. The browser is a thin renderer - no dagre, no Mermaid, no layout in the client.
steps.detail: That is what makes the picture reproducible: the same repo in gives a byte-identical graph out, so a diff between two runs is meaningful.

node.label: Place the geometry
node.oneLiner: Deterministic React Flow geometry.

steps.title: Geometry is a server concern

steps.body: The spine is the longest reachable path through a lane, and it gets the straight line. Everything else is offset into a column beside it - exactly like this page.
steps.detail: The layout you are looking at right now is the same idea applied by hand: a main line down the middle, branches to either side, converging back.

node.label: Is this node on the spine?
node.oneLiner: The longest path gets the straight line.

steps.title: Decision - spine, or branch?

steps.body: A skeleton of at most 15 nodes, with every other decision one + away. On django-helpdesk that is 222 decisions sitting behind this same surface.
steps.detail: Positions come from the render agent, so the frontend only decides what is revealed - never where anything goes.

node.label: The diagram you are looking at
node.oneLiner: 15 visible nodes, everything else one + away.

steps.title: And this is the output

steps.body: Progressive disclosure is the last decision in the system, and it belongs to the reader. This tour is itself a CodeFlow diagram - click any node to open its source.

branches.label: expand
branches.note: The camera flies to what was revealed.

steps.detail: Both arms stop here, because this is where the pipeline hands over. Everything you have seen was hand-authored as a FlowGraph and run through the real placer - the same code path a real repo takes.

data.code:
for start in range(0, len(representatives), _BATCH_SIZE):
    batch = representatives[start : start + _BATCH_SIZE]
    batch_verdicts = self._judge_batch(batch)
    for candidate in batch:
        fingerprint = fingerprints[candidate.site_id]
        verdict = batch_verdicts[candidate.site_id]
        self._cache.put(fingerprint, verdict)
        for duplicate in groups[fingerprint]:
            results[duplicate.site_id] = verdict
self._cache.flush()
return results
data.oneLiner: Batches representatives, then fans the verdict back out to every duplicate fork sharing that fingerprint.
